opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most exciting implications of continual learning, and also one of the least appreciated.

Right now, when you talk to a language model, almost everything it knows about you lives in the context window. You can stuff in a long history, you can add retrieval, you can write a little memory file, but the model's parameters are frozen. It's the same model for you as for everyone else, and it starts every conversation the same way. Its personalization is a kind of short-term memory taped onto a fixed long-term memory. In the brain, that would look a lot like anterograde amnesia. You can hold things in working memory, but nothing gets consolidated.

Continual learning changes that picture because the model can update some part of itself at test time based on what it experiences. In our work on architectures like Titans, and more broadly in the nested learning view, we think of memory as a spectrum. Some components update very fast, almost token by token, some update more slowly, and some are close to the frozen pretraining knowledge. Once you have that hierarchy, interacting with a user isn't just filling a buffer. Information can flow from the fast memory into slower, more persistent memory, and it gets compressed in the process.

For individual users, that means a few things. First, the model can learn *you* rather than just store transcripts of you. It can pick up how you like explanations framed, which assumptions you already share, what your codebase or research area looks like, and fold that into how it processes new inputs, instead of retrieving a snippet and hoping it's relevant. Second, it should scale better over time. Context windows and retrieval get expensive and noisy as history grows, while a learned memory can abstract and decide what's surprising and worth keeping and what can be forgotten. Surprise-based updating is a big part of how we think about this. Third, adaptation becomes cumulative. Each interaction makes the next one a bit better, which is much closer to how a human collaborator gets better at working with you over months.

I should be honest about the hard parts. Catastrophic forgetting is still real. You don't want a model that adapts to one user's quirks and loses general capabilities. That's partly why the multi-timescale design matters: you want the personal adaptation to happen in the right layers of memory, not to overwrite everything. There are also serious questions about privacy and isolation. If the model is updating its weights based on your data, you need guarantees about where those updates live and that they don't leak to other users. And there's a safety and alignment angle. A model that keeps learning after deployment is a moving target, so evaluation can't be a one-time snapshot anymore.

But directionally, I think we move from "one model, many prompts" to something closer to "one base model, many continually adapting instances," where the model you're talking to after a year really is shaped by that year of working with you. That's a qualitatively different kind of personalization than anything we have today.

r001.rationale: It says the model can learn each user’s preferences, such as how they like explanations framed, and use that learning to process future inputs, supporting answers tailored to different users.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that it changes the whole relationship between the model and the person using it. Right now, when you talk to a language model, it has a fixed set of weights that were frozen at the end of pretraining or post-training, and everything it knows about you has to live in the context window. The moment the conversation ends, or the context fills up, that's gone. So every interaction is, in some sense, a first date. The model has to be reminded who you are, what you care about, how you like things explained.

Continual learning, at least the way we think about it, is about giving the model a memory that actually updates its parameters, or some part of its parameters, as it interacts with you. Not just storing tokens, but genuinely compressing experience into the weights. And once you have that, the model can start to specialize to an individual. It can learn that you're a physicist who prefers derivations over analogies, or that you always want the code in Rust, or that when you say "make it shorter" you mean cut it in half, not trim a sentence. Those are things a human assistant picks up after a week of working with you, and today's models essentially never pick them up.

I'd point to a few concrete shifts. First, personalization becomes implicit rather than explicit. You don't have to write a system prompt describing yourself; the model infers your preferences from the history of interactions and adapts. Second, the model can learn facts about your world that it had no way of knowing from pretraining: your project, your codebase, your family, the vocabulary of your field. And third, and this is the one I find most interesting, the model can learn how you learn. If it explains something and you push back, that signal can actually change how it approaches similar explanations next time, not just within the session but permanently.

Now, there are real challenges. The obvious one is catastrophic forgetting: you don't want the model to become so specialized to you that it loses its general competence. There's also the question of what to remember versus what to forget. Not everything you say should be written into long-term memory. A good memory system is selective; it's surprised by things that matter and ignores the noise. A lot of our work on architectures like Titans is really about that: how do you decide, at test time, what's worth memorizing, and how do you do it efficiently without going back and retraining the whole thing.

But if you get that right, I think the experience of using a model goes from talking to a very knowledgeable stranger to working with a collaborator that has actually been paying attention. And that's a qualitatively different thing.

r001.rationale: The response says continual learning lets a model specialize to an individual and adapt to that person’s preferences, including how explanations are presented, which communicates tailoring answers to users’ differing expectations.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that the model can learn from its interactions with you, rather than treating every interaction as a fresh start. It can gradually understand how you like things explained, what you already know, and what kinds of help you need. So two users could ask the same question and get different answers—not because the underlying facts are different, but because the explanation is adapted to each person.

But the important part is deciding what to learn and what to retain. Something you say once might be a temporary preference, or it might be a correction that should change future responses. A continually learning model needs to distinguish those things and remain able to adapt when you change your mind. The goal is an assistant that becomes more useful through experience with you, while still letting you control what it remembers.

r001.rationale: The response says two users can receive different answers to the same question because the model adapts its explanation to each person’s preferences, knowledge, and needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that the model can actually learn from its interaction with you. Today, most personalization happens through the context: you provide some information, or the system retrieves a memory and puts it into the prompt. That’s useful, but it’s different from the model adapting through experience.

With continual learning, the model could gradually learn how you communicate, what you already know, and what kind of explanation is useful to you. If you correct it, ideally that correction changes its future behavior, so you don’t have to keep repeating yourself. The interaction becomes more like an ongoing collaboration.

But the challenge is deciding what to learn and what to retain. Something you say once might be a temporary preference, or it might be important for every future conversation. And learning something new shouldn’t erase something useful from before. So the opportunity is much deeper personalization, but it depends on getting that balance between adaptation and memory right.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning an individual user’s communication style and preferred explanations, but it does not clearly state that the model would tailor answers differently for different users asking the same question.
